items.readable_text:
Content:
Remember that if [MATH: X] is a binomial random variable in which there are [MATH: n] experiments and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment, then [MATH: X] has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}.]

Content:
It can be shown that the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of a binomial random variable [MATH: X] can be computed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: E[X]|= np; Var[X]|= np(1 − p); SD[X]|= sqrt(np(1 − p))]

items.title: Finding the Mean of a Binomial Random Variable

sections.normalized_html: A coin is biased so that the probability of it landing on heads is [MATH: 0.4.] The coin is tossed [MATH: 7] times. What is the mean number of times the coin lands on heads?
sections.readable_text: A coin is biased so that the probability of it landing on heads is [MATH: 0.4.] The coin is tossed [MATH: 7] times. What is the mean number of times the coin lands on heads?

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of times the coin lands on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=7] tosses

  • the probability of landing on heads for each toss is [MATH: p=0.4]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(7,0.4).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: X,] the mean is given by [MATH: \textrm E[X] = np,] where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean of the number of times the coin lands on heads is

[MATH: E[X]|= np; = (7)(0.4); = 2.8.]

items.title: Finding the Variance of a Binomial Random Variable

sections.normalized_html: An archer practices shooting [MATH: 12] arrows at a target. The archer has a [MATH: 50\%] chance of hitting the bull's eye. What is the variance in the number of arrows that hit the bull's eye?
sections.readable_text: An archer practices shooting [MATH: 12] arrows at a target. The archer has a [MATH: 50\%] chance of hitting the bull's eye. What is the variance in the number of arrows that hit the bull's eye?

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of arrows that hit the bull's eye.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=12] shots

  • the probability of hitting the bull's eye for each arrow is [MATH: p=50\%=0.5]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(12,0.5).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: X,] the variance is given by [MATH: \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p),] where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of arrows hitting the bull's eye is

[MATH: Var[X]|= np(1 − p); = (12)(0.5)(1 − 0.5); = (6)(0.5); = 3.]

items.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

sections.normalized_html: A fair five-sided die is rolled [MATH: 8] times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: A fair five-sided die is rolled [MATH: 8] times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=8] rolls of the die

  • the probability of getting an even number (i.e., a [MATH: 2,] or [MATH: 4]) on any roll of the die is [MATH: p=\dfrac{2}{5} .]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B\left(8,\dfrac25\right).]

For a binomial random variable [MATH: X,] the standard deviation is given by [MATH: \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},] where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number is [MATH: SD[X]|= sqrt(np(1 − p)); = sqrt(8 ⋅ (2)/(5) ⋅ (1 − (2)/(5))); = sqrt(1.92); = 1.386] rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
